results.result: Eight X-linked D. mauritiana segments covering ~85% of the X chromosome were introgressed into D. simulans. All eight 2P introgression genotypes were completely male-sterile, while the successful generation of these lines confirmed no dominant female-lethal factors. Recombinant 1P-YFP genotypes (n=617) showed a range of fertility phenotypes, with 38.6% completely sterile and 13.9% having fertility indistinguishable from controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C43 provide comprehensive experimental evidence from the introgression mapping approach. The successful generation of female-viable lines (C32), complete male sterility of all 2P lines (C33), and detailed fertility phenotyping of 617 recombinant genotypes (C35-C40) with genome-wide genotyping confirmation (C41-C43) collectively support this result. The data are internally consistent and methodologically sound.

results.result: High-resolution genetic mapping identified at least six genetically separable regions on the D. mauritiana X chromosome that cause hybrid male sterility. Three large regions can be introgressed without strong fertility effects, while four small regions (<700 kb) consistently and strongly reduce male fertility. QTL analysis confirmed at least five significant peaks (p<0.01) affecting male fertility.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 and C119 are well-supported by the fertility mapping data shown in Figures 2-3. The identification of both permissive and restrictive regions is based on systematic phenotyping of recombinant genotypes. Claims C124-C126 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the mapping approach, noting this provides a minimum estimate. The statistical support (C46) and effect size estimates (C47) strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Fertile 1P-YFP males showed male-biased progeny sex ratios (mean proportion daughters = 0.45), with 86% of genotypes producing <50% daughters. This bias was partially attributable to the sim wXD1 background. A significant negative correlation existed between introgression length and proportion of female progeny (ρ = -0.31, p<0.0001), independent of fertility effects, suggesting the Y chromosome of sim wXD1 causes weak segregation distortion modified by X-linked D. mauritiana alleles.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C55 present consistent evidence for sex ratio distortion. The observation is supported by appropriate controls (C50), statistical analyses including correlation and partial correlation (C51, C53, C54), and comparison with control genotypes. The interpretation (C55) is reasonable given the data, though it remains somewhat speculative. The independence of the introgression length effect from fertility (C54) strengthens the inference of drive modification.

results.result: A novel cryptic X-linked drive locus was discovered in D. mauritiana in the distal 2P-5 region. Introgressions including this region produced female-biased progeny (54.6% daughters for mauritiana allele vs. 42.5% for simulans allele). This region does not contain previously mapped D. simulans drive loci, representing the first evidence of cryptic X-chromosome drive in D. mauritiana.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 and C142-C143 provide convergent evidence for a novel drive locus. The QTL mapping (C57), effect size estimation (C58), comparison with parental strain phenotypes (C60), and exclusion of known D. simulans drive loci (C61) collectively support the discovery. The inference of a cryptic drive allele (C59, C62) is reasonable given the female-biased sex ratios observed only when introgressed into a naive genetic background.

results.result: Population genomic analyses revealed that D. mauritiana has a smaller effective population size than D. simulans. D. mauritiana showed 32% lower X-chromosomal and 19% lower autosomal polymorphism, retained 74.4% as many ancestral polymorphisms, accumulated 46.3% as many derived polymorphisms, had less negatively skewed site frequency spectra, and exhibited twofold higher linkage disequilibrium compared to D. simulans.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C70 present multiple convergent lines of population genetic evidence consistently indicating smaller effective population size in D. mauritiana. The statistics (nucleotide diversity, ancestral/derived SNP ratios, Tajima's D, linkage disequilibrium) are standard and appropriately applied. The findings are consistent with previous studies (C63 cites supporting work) and with expectations for an island-endemic species. The X/autosome ratio analysis (C65-C66) provides additional support.

results.result: Interspecific divergence and differentiation analyses showed median DXY of 0.010 (X) and 0.013 (autosomes), with net divergence (DA) significantly greater on the X (0.0007) than autosomes (-0.0005). FST was higher for the X (0.378) than autosomes (0.279), implying mean coalescence times for between-species gene copies are 2.2-fold (X) and 1.8-fold (autosomes) deeper than within-species coalescence times.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 present standard population genetic statistics appropriately calculated and interpreted. The explanation for negative autosomal DA (C73) is correct. The statistical significance of X vs. autosome differences (C74, C75) is properly tested. The inference of coalescence time ratios from FST (C76, C77) is appropriately cited to Slatkin 1993. The pattern of greater X chromosome differentiation is consistent with the large X-effect and reduced X-linked gene flow.

results.result: Genome-wide Gmin analysis identified 196 10-kb windows (1.9%) with significantly low values indicating recent introgression, corresponding to 48 total introgressions (27 small 10-kb, 21 larger 20-280 kb). Introgressions were 4.4-fold underrepresented on the X chromosome (1 X-linked vs. 47 autosomal). Introgression characteristics showed signatures of recombinational erosion over time and dependence on local recombination rates, with 2-5% of the genome showing evidence of introgression.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C92, C132, and C135 present a comprehensive introgression analysis using the Gmin statistic. The Monte Carlo simulation approach for significance testing (C81) is appropriate. The underrepresentation of X-linked introgressions (C86, C89) is statistically significant and biologically meaningful. The correlations between introgression length, Gmin values, Dxy, and recombination rate (C90-C92) provide mechanistic insights. The consistency between 5-kb and 10-kb window analyses (C135) validates the approach.

results.result: The single X-linked introgression corresponds to a ~130-kb region containing the Winters sex-ratio drive genes MDox and Dox. This region showed a 2.4-fold reduction in Gmin (0.333 vs. background 0.785), extremely low minimum DXY (0.00087), and elevated Patterson's D (0.4382 vs. 0.1054 for rest of X), indicating recent gene flow between species at this locus.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 provide multiple convergent lines of evidence for introgression at the MDox-Dox locus. The Gmin analysis (C95), minimum DXY calculation, and ABBA-BABA test (C97-C99) all independently support recent gene flow. The statistical significance of differences between this region and genomic background (C98) strengthens the conclusion. The identification of this specific region as containing known drive genes (C94) is factually correct and sets up the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: The MDox-Dox drive system shows evidence of introgression-mediated selective sweeps in both species. In D. mauritiana, nucleotide diversity in this region is 24% of background levels. MDox and Dox are overrepresented among shared haplotypes between species (6/7 shared haplotypes have MDox/Dox, p=0.0018). The probability of random co-localization of a 130-kb introgression with MDox-Dox is 0.004. MDox is expressed in testes of both species, and segregation distortion mediated by these genes likely drove the introgression and parallel sweeps.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C114 build a compelling case for drive-mediated introgression. The prior characterization of MDox/Dox function (C101-C104) is properly cited. The permutation test (C105) demonstrates non-random co-localization. The sweep signatures in both species (C107-C108) are well-documented. The overrepresentation of MDox/Dox in shared haplotypes (C110-C111) with statistical support is strong evidence. The expression data (C113) confirms potential activity. The hypothesis (C106, C114) is well-supported though remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The MDox-Dox introgression co-localizes with one of three X-chromosomal regions that does not cause male sterility when introgressed from D. mauritiana into D. simulans. This driving haplotype swept to high frequency in D. simulans and fixation in D. mauritiana, reducing local sequence divergence and undermining the accumulation of genetic incompatibilities that might cause hybrid male sterility in this region.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 integrate the sterility mapping and introgression analyses to reach a key conclusion. The co-localization of the MDox-Dox introgression with a sterility-free region (C115) is directly supported by Figures 2 and 6. The inference that the drive element reduced divergence and undermined sterility evolution (C116, C118) is well-supported by the reduced Gmin, low divergence, and absence of sterility factors. This represents a novel finding that gene flow at a drive locus can counteract, rather than promote, reproductive isolation.

results.result: After ~250,000 years of divergence, sufficient X-linked hybrid male sterility has accumulated to render most of the D. mauritiana X chromosome male-sterile on a D. simulans genetic background. This high density of genetic incompatibilities corresponds with a dearth of gene flow on the X chromosome. The combination of extensive reproductive isolation with modest genetic divergence makes this species pair ideal for studying speciation genetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C29, and C120-C122 synthesize the major findings. The high density of incompatibilities (C3) is supported by the sterility mapping showing most of the X causes sterility. The reduced X-linked gene flow (C4) is supported by the introgression analysis showing 4.4-fold underrepresentation. The temporal context (C120) is supported by cited divergence time estimates. The characterization as an ideal system (C122) is a reasonable inference given the documented patterns.

results.result: The mapping experiments provide no direct evidence that sex-ratio distortion causes hybrid male sterility, as no sterility loci co-localized with sex-ratio loci. However, the experiments revealed new evidence for cryptic drive systems. Four cryptic drive systems have been identified across D. simulans and D. mauritiana, regarded as a minimum number due to detection limitations. The discovery of multiple alternative cryptic drive systems implies sex chromosome drive is not infrequent during species divergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C146 appropriately acknowledge both negative and positive findings regarding the drive theory. The lack of co-localization (C137) is honestly reported. The explanation for difficulty detecting drive in sterile males (C138-C139) is logical. The discovery of a novel D. mauritiana drive locus (C141) is supported by earlier claims. The enumeration of four systems (C144) and acknowledgment of this being a minimum (C145) with clear reasoning is appropriate. The inference about frequency of drive (C146) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: The Winters sex-ratio drivers MDox and Dox migrated between D. mauritiana and D. simulans, despite being suppressed by Nmy in both species. This finding reveals that the drive theory's implicit assumption of strict allopatry may not hold. For introgression to occur, MDox/Dox alleles must not have caused sterility, no tightly linked sterility factors prevented recombinational escape, and any sterility factors in the introgressed region were replaced. This suggests a selfish drive system invaded a new species without causing male sterility and may have impeded hybrid sterility evolution in this region.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C158 present a well-reasoned synthesis of the implications. The introgression of MDox-Dox (C147) is well-established by prior claims. The presence of Nmy in both species (C148) is cited. The alternative hypotheses for suppression (C149) and acknowledgment of inability to distinguish them (C150) is appropriately cautious. The logical conditions for introgression (C155-C157) are sound. The inference about drive theory assumptions (C151) and the conclusion about drive undermining sterility evolution (C158) are well-supported, though the latter remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The manuscript situates the work within established speciation genetics theory, including Haldane's rule, the large X-effect, and the drive theory. Sex chromosomes often accumulate interspecific genetic incompatibilities faster than autosomes. The drive theory posits that sex chromosomes are susceptible to recurrent meiotic drive and suppression, causing divergent cryptic drive systems and genetic incompatibilities. Multiple lines of evidence support the plausibility of the drive theory, including widespread drive systems, co-localization of drive and sterility loci, and dual-function genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C8-C21 provide appropriate theoretical and empirical context from the literature. These are well-established patterns (C9-C13) and theories (C2, C14-C17) properly cited. The evidence for plausibility of drive theory (C18-C21) is appropriately cited to prior work. These claims establish the conceptual framework for the study and are supported by extensive literature citations. They represent accurate summaries of prior knowledge rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: D. mauritiana and D. simulans diverged ~240,000 years ago, with D. mauritiana originating from a D. simulans-like ancestor on Madagascar that colonized Mauritius. The species are geographically isolated and reproductively incompatible (F1 males sterile, F1 females fertile), yet show clear evidence of historical gene flow. The coalescent history reaches deeper than the species split time. Theoretical considerations predict that foreign haplotypes must escape disfavored backgrounds by recombination before elimination by selection, with X-linked haplotypes facing greater constraints.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C28, C30, C78, C128-C131, and C133 provide essential background on the study system. The divergence times (C22-C23), geographic isolation (C24), reproductive barriers (C25-C27), and historical gene flow (C28, C78) are all properly cited to prior work. The coalescent history (C129) is supported by the current study's data. The theoretical expectations about introgression (C130-C131, C133) are appropriately cited. These claims accurately represent the study system and relevant theory.

results.result: The authors acknowledge several limitations of their approaches. The 2P mapping scheme, while designed to facilitate sterility factor identification, cannot determine the number of sterility factors in regions where strong factors are close to both flanking markers. The experiments provide only a minimum estimate of total sterility factors and likely miss small-effect factors. The 10-kb Gmin windows likely fail to identify very small or old introgressions.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 and C134 appropriately acknowledge methodological limitations. The limitation regarding 2P-6 (C125) is a logical consequence of the experimental design. The acknowledgment that this provides a minimum estimate (C126) and likely misses small-effect factors (C127) is scientifically appropriate. The limitation of the Gmin window size (C134) is reasonable. These represent honest and appropriate caveats that strengthen rather than weaken the overall conclusions.

results.result: The original drive theory posits that hybrid incompatibilities accumulate as incidental by-products of recurrent bouts of meiotic drive and suppression.
results.evaluation: Claim C136 accurately states the drive theory as formulated by Hurst and Pomiankowski (1991) and Frank (1991), properly cited. This is an accurate representation of established theory.
